item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Tue Sep 22 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Spy Training 101: Decode a Secret Message — Tue Sep 22 — North Carolina Museum of Natural Sciences
item.description:
Pretend you’ve been recruited as a member of the Culper Spy Ring, and you need to know how to decipher a message written in invisible ink. Supplies include a paint brush, water, drying cloth, vitriol (diluted sulfuric acid), Thomas Jefferson cipher and “furnace box.” Read the clues to find the coin with a hidden message, reveal the message using the brush and vitriol, then use the cipher to decode the message.
Contact: Nancy Locquet Absillis, nancy.locquet@naturalsciences.org

item.title: The Battle of Shallow Ford: An Exhibition of Watercolors and Words — Tue Sep 22 — Welborn Gallery
item.description:
On Display September 3 – Octobe 30, 2026
This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. The words are researched through works including “Records of the Moravians” and NC State Archives. This exhibition is presented in partnership with The Lewisville Area Arts Council and was supported by the America 250 NC Community Grant.
An opening reception will be held September 3 from 5-7pm at the Yadkin Cultural Arts Center.
Refreshments will be served.
Free Admission, all are welcome to attend.

item.title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence — Tue Sep 22, 10:00 AM — Kings Mountain Historical Museum
item.description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.
The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Tue Sep 22, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: FIP Seminar: Label-Free Chemical Imaging of Single-Cell Drug Response: From Subcellular Quantification to Super-Resolution — Wed Sep 23, 12:00 PM — Wilkinson 021
item.description:
Drug discovery demands measurements that capture tumor heterogeneity, yet conventional assays report only ensemble averages. Stimulated Raman scattering (SRS) microscopy addresses this gap by directly probing drug distribution and phenotypic state in single cells, label-free and quantitatively. I will show how SRS enables longitudinal, subcellular measurement of drug uptake and efficacy in 2D cultures and 3D tumor spheroids, with machine learning applied to classify cell type and state from the resulting SRS images for content-rich screening. To further elevate SRS capabilities for this application, I will present two orthogonal advances: a 4Pi-SRS interferometric scheme that improves axial resolution nearly sevenfold, and computational reconstruction methods that enhance spatial resolution and accelerate volumetric imaging. Together, these tools chart a route toward high-throughput, high-content, label-free drug screening in physiologically relevant models.
Source: Duke University

Abstract: Nanomaterials have found widespread use in a broad range of applications, including photonics, electronics, catalysis, energy conversion, sensing, imaging, and biomedicine. For almost three decades, my research group has been working diligently to develop chemical methods for the synthesis and fabrication of novel nanomaterials with well-controlled properties. Some of these nanomaterials have also been successfully commercialized. In this talk, I will briefly review my journey into this exciting field of research. item.description: Abstract: As in-patient environments generate vast amounts of heterogeneous data, ranging from continuous physiological telemetry to sparsely sampled medical imaging, there is a profound opportunity to translate this information into actionable clinical foresight. This talk will focus on the development of novel foundation models and transformer architectures designed to handle the temporal complexities of longitudinal hospital data. item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Thu Sep 24 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.description:

This collection of “watercolors” by master craftsman Rick Jones is accompanied by storyboards of “words” by artist and writer, Marilyn Ingram. The story, unfolding during a time where there were no cameras, cell phones, or even a typewriter, is told through the eyes of artists, field correspondents who would paint, draw or write a journal. The paintings include scenes at the Shallow Ford and nearby battle area, Moravian settlements along the great wagon road, and annual commemoration in Huntsville, NC. item.title: Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & The Fight for Independence — Thu Sep 24, 10:00 AM — Kings Mountain Historical Museum
item.description:
In partnership with the Catawba Cultural Center, Kings Mountain Historical Museum is excited to present, "Choosing Sides: The Catawba Nation & the Fight for Independence." This exhibit explores the critical role of the Catawba Nation, also known as Yį Iswąre or “People of the River,” in the American Revolutionary War, particularly in the backcountry regions of Tryon and Lincoln Counties. As skilled warriors, guides, and allies of the Patriot cause, the Catawba people defended their homeland, protected settler communities, and contributed to pivotal battles. Despite the hardships of disease, displacement, and warfare, the Catawba demonstrated extraordinary resilience. Their story is one of courage, alliance, and survival, woven into the struggle for independence in the Southern Campaign of the Revolution.
The exhibit will run from June 30, 2026 until October 24, 2026. Admission is Free!
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Thu Sep 24, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

Gather and unwind to the NC-borne songs and spirit of Kit McKay from 6:00–8:00 pm. Food truck service begins at 5:00 pm.
Patrick Stovall, known as Kit McKay in his latest solo project, offers a refreshingly free approach to music-making, entertaining the ridiculous as well as the profound. His recent release, The Dirt Candies, perfectly embodies this philosophy. What started as weekend jam sessions with his college roommate, Matt Southern, has become an unexpected calling card. The deliberately silly songs have caught the attention of college radio stations and audiences hungry for something real.
Park Hangs
Join us to unwind and socialize at a new outdoor concert series with music by NC-based artists, food and drinks by local vendors, and easygoing vibes in Bailey Park (445 Patterson Ave. in Winston-Salem). Celebrate National Public Lands Day with a Tails & Trails Quest!
Looking for a fun way to celebrate National Public Lands Day? Join us for the next Tails & Trails Quest on Saturday, September 26 at 10:00 am presented by Friends of the Fonta Flora State Trail and Lake James State Park.
This self-guided adventure takes place along the Holly Discovery Trail, a scenic, family-friendly, one-mile loop that's perfect for hikers of all ages (and their four-legged friends!).
Along the trail you'll discover: - Interactive educational stations - A fun quest to complete Fascinating facts about the plants, wildlife, and natural history of Lake James - Learn more about the growing Fonta Flora State Trail and how it's connecting communities across Western North Carolina.
Whether you're exploring with your kids, walking the dog, or simply looking for a beautiful way to spend the day outdoors, this event is designed to help you connect with nature while supporting the future of trails in our region

item.title: National Public Lands Day Hike — Sat Sep 26, 10:30 AM — Hammocks Beach State Park
item.description:
Join a Ranger for a guided hike in celebration of National Public Lands Day! Discover the park's natural beauty, learn about local wildlife and coastal ecosystems, and help protect our public lands by picking up litter along the way. Hike will follow the Coastal Fringe and Hickory Bluff Trails for ~2.5 miles. Pack water and gloves! Meet at the trailhead.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Carolina Blues: Indigo on the Cape Fear — Sat Sep 26, 11:00 AM — North Carolina Maritime Museum at Southport
item.description:
Don’t be blue – we have lots of indigo for you! This subtropical plant was an incredibly important commodity in the Carolinas of the 18th century. We will be exploring the process used by skilled enslaved African labor to extract this valuable dye from the indigo plants - and delve into the science behind dye production. Visitors will have a chance to view and work an active fermentation vat, and dyeing demonstrations will occur throughout the course of the program. T-shirts will also be available for purchase for visitors to try their hand at resist dyeing.
This is a partnered program between Brunswick Town/Fort Anderson State Historic Site and the North Carolina Maritime Museum at Southport. In 2026, this event will be held at the North Carolina Maritime Museum at Southport.
This is an America 250 NC event.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Fort Macon Daily Tours - 11 am, 1 pm, & 3 pm — Sat Sep 26, 11:00 AM — Fort Macon State Park
item.description:
Guided tours of Fort Macon are available daily at 11:00 a.m., 1:00 p.m., and 3:00 p.m. during the summer season from mid April to mid Oct.
On Cannon days there will only be one Fort Tour scheduled at 12:00 noon.
Tours last about 45 minutes.
Meet at the fort entrance. Pets are not allowed inside the fort.
Photo by C. Peek: The fort at Fort Macon State Park
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: History on Tap: The Wolfpack Brewing Lab — Sat Sep 26, 11:00 AM — Main Foyer
item.description:
Speaker: Sebastian Wolfrum, Lecturer and Brewing Laboratory Manager, Food, Bioprocessing and Nutrition Sciences, NC State University
Location: Main Foyer, Schaub Hall, 400 Dan Allen Dr., NC State University, Raleigh, NC 27606
Description: Curious about how beer is made, how it all got started, and how the next generation of brewers are learning the craft that is the basis of modern bioprocessing? Join us for a special behind-the-scenes tour of the Wolfpack Brewing Lab at NC State and learn how the grain-to-glass magic happens! Whether you’re a microbrew enthusiast or just curious about the history and science of fermentation, you won’t want to miss this.
Spots are limited, so grab a ticket and come see what the Wolfpack Brewing Lab is all about!
For questions, please contact Stacey Smith (919)-814-7032.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Junior Ranger Discovery Hike — Sat Sep 26, 11:00 AM — Haw River State Park - Iron Ore Belt Access
item.description:
Calling all young explorers! On National Public Lands Day (9/26) and as part of Take A Child Outside Week (Sept 24-30), meet a park ranger at The Iron Ore Belt Access for a leisurely hike that mixes science, history, and conservation. Paticipants will be issued a junior ranger booklet at the trailhead and guidance for working through the activities with the goal of earning the park's junior ranger patch by the end of our adventure. Plan for a 1.5-2.0 mile, relatively-flat hike over natural surface trails, mostly shaded but with potential for some open, sunny areas. No two hikes are ever alike... What will you discover on our walk through the woods?
Please wear close-toed shoes, a hat or umbrella for sun protection if you like, and bring bottled water plus whatever you need to be comfortable for a two-hour nature walk.
